column1: What is the "Framework of the Opposites"?
column2: For every decision, consider the exact opposite (push vs pull, store vs don't store, build vs offload), evaluate all paths, then choose.

column1: Why does a presence system use client heartbeats instead of the server polling clients?
column2: Without a persistent connection the server cannot reach the client, so the client must push a periodic pulse.

column1: What should the presence table store: a boolean or a timestamp?
column2: The last heartbeat time (epoch). Online = now − last_hb is below a threshold (e.g. 30 s).

column1: Storage for 1B users at 8 bytes per row?
column2: About 8 GB (4 B user_id + 4 B last_hb).

column1: How does "absence == offline" shrink the presence store?
column2: Keep rows only for active users and expire them by TTL. 100k active × 8 B ≈ 800 KB instead of 8 GB.

column1: Two ways to delete expired presence rows? Which is better?
column2: A CRON job you run, or offloading to a datastore with native TTL (Redis/DynamoDB). Offloading is simpler.

column1: Redis vs DynamoDB for presence: what decides?
column2: Context: Redis is fast in-memory but costly and self-run; DynamoDB is durable, managed, multi-region, cheaper, with AWS lock-in.

column1: Heartbeat every 10 s with 1M active users: DB write rate?
column2: 6M writes per minute (100k per second).

column1: Why does connection pooling matter for tiny DB updates?
column2: TCP setup/teardown per request dominates; reusing pre-established connections removes it.

column1: What data structure implements a connection pool?
column2: A bounded blocking queue (often a circular array) of connection objects; borrowers wait when it's empty.

column1: Reasons for soft delete?
column2: Recoverability, archival, audit, and no B+ tree rebalancing that a real DELETE can cause.

column1: What is a cache stampede and the fix?
column2: Many concurrent misses on one key all hit the DB. Request coalescing (single-flight): one request fetches, the rest wait for its result.

column1: Vertical vs horizontal scaling: what does horizontal add?
column2: Near-linear capacity increase and fault tolerance (vertical just makes one box bigger).

column1: Why scale bottom-up?
column2: Stateful layers (DB, cache) must handle the concurrent load from all API servers; scale them first.

column1: Three ways to scale a relational DB?
column2: Vertical scaling, read replicas, sharding (plus a proxy to route).

column1: What does a DB proxy like ProxySQL do?
column2: Knows the topology; routes queries via rules (e.g. SELECT → replica hostgroup), pools connections, can cache.

column1: The performance mantra for delegation?
column2: What doesn't need to be done in realtime shouldn't be done in realtime.

column1: Which tasks should be delegated to async workers?
column2: Long-running tasks, heavy computation, batch writes, anything eventually consistent.

column1: Message queue vs message stream?
column2: Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ): each message goes to one consumer. Stream (Kafka, Kinesis): each consumer group reads every message.

column1: Why use Kafka instead of one worker that counts and indexes?
column2: Separation of concerns: separate consumer groups (counter, search) each process the same event.

column1: Kafka's ordering guarantee?
column2: Only within a partition; none across partitions.

column1: Two Kafka partition limitations?
column2: You can't reduce partitions; consumers in a group beyond the partition count sit idle.

column1: Short polling vs long polling?
column2: Short: server responds immediately, client repeats. Long: server holds the request until data is ready or timeout.

column1: WebSockets vs SSE?
column2: WebSockets: bidirectional persistent channel. SSE: server-to-client one-way stream over HTTP.

column1: Typical load sequence for a realtime app?
column2: Load UI → fetch initial state via REST → subscribe to live updates.

column1: Pessimistic locking flow?
column2: Acquire lock → read/update → release (on commit or rollback).

column1: Why do databases need locks?
column2: To protect data consistency and integrity under concurrent updates.

column1: FOR UPDATE vs SKIP LOCKED vs NOWAIT on a locked row?
column2: Wait · skip it and return other rows · fail immediately with an error.

column1: Why use SKIP LOCKED for airline seat selection?
column2: Users need any free seat; concurrent transactions each grab a different unlocked seat without queueing or double booking.

column1: Name systems with "fixed inventory + contention".
column2: Airline check-in, CoWIN slots, IRCTC, BookMyShow, flash sales.

column1: How do you avoid an is_deleted column in the KV store?
column2: Use a sentinel: expired_at = -1 marks a deleted row.

column1: How is PUT implemented in the KV store?
column2: An upsert (MySQL REPLACE INTO / ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE; Postgres ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE), not GET-then-INSERT/UPDATE.

column1: How does GET respect TTL?
column2: WHERE key = k AND expired_at > NOW(). Expired rows are filtered at read time.

column1: Why add LIMIT 1000 to the cleanup DELETE?
column2: Avoid huge transactions that hold many locks, bloat logs, lag replicas and stall live traffic.

column1: When are read replicas appropriate?
column2: Read-heavy load where slightly stale reads are fine; send consistent reads to the master.

column1: Master can't handle writes: what next?
column2: Scale vertically first; then shard (range or hash) so each master owns an exclusive slice of keys.

column1: Do FOR UPDATE locks block a plain SELECT in InnoDB/Postgres?
column2: No. Plain reads use MVCC snapshots; only locking reads wait.

column1: What do most NoSQL DBs trade for scalability and availability?
column2: Consistency (most are eventually consistent).

column1: Does "NoSQL scales" imply "SQL doesn't"?
column2: No. Anything you can shard scales, relational DBs included.

column1: Document vs key-value store?
column2: Document: JSON, complex queries, partial updates (MongoDB). KV: key-wise access, heavily partitioned, no complex queries (Redis, DynamoDB).

column1: Why are column stores used for analytics?
column2: They read only the columns a query touches, not whole rows.

column1: Wide-column store in one line?
column2: Columns grouped into column families stored together on disk across rows (Cassandra).

column1: Slack insight 1?
column2: A DM is just a channel with two members.

column1: How are Slack messages sharded and why?
column2: By workspace, so all of a workspace's history is on one shard (no cross-shard scrolling).

column1: What does membership.checkpoint store and why?
column2: Last message id read; the client fetches anything newer, which recovers missed realtime messages.

column1: Persistence-first vs realtime-first chat examples?
column2: Slack persists first; WhatsApp delivers realtime with async persistence; Zoom chat has no persistence.

column1: Why multiplex everything over one WebSocket per user?
column2: WebSockets are expensive persistent TCP connections and browsers limit them.

column1: How do edge servers deliver across servers?
column2: Each subscribes to Redis Pub/Sub channels (one per Slack channel) for its users; publishes fan out to every subscribed edge.

column1: What does a TCP connection's identity consist of?
column2: Source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol.

column1: Why do LB servers keep config in memory?
column2: A config-DB call per request would wreck latency; the in-memory copy is kept in sync.

column1: How does config reach LB servers quickly, and what if that path fails?
column2: Config DB → CDC → Redis Pub/Sub push; if Pub/Sub is down, LBs poll.

column1: What does the LB orchestrator do?
column2: Health-checks backends and LB servers, updates the backend list, scales LB servers using metrics from Prometheus.

column1: How is the orchestrator itself kept alive?
column2: Leader election: a master assigns exclusive work to workers; a new master is elected on failure.

column1: How do you scale the LB tier itself?
column2: Weighted DNS (e.g. CoreDNS) resolving one name to many LB server IPs.

column1: How do two DNS servers provide HA without client changes?
column2: They share a Virtual IP via VRRP; the secondary takes over the VIP (ARP) when the primary fails.

column1: How do threads, processes and machines synchronise?
column2: Mutex/semaphore; disk (lock files); remote lock manager.

column1: Two requirements for a remote lock manager?
column2: Atomic acquire and automatic expiry (TTL).

column1: Redis command to acquire a lock with expiry?
column2: SET key owner NX EX ttl (set-if-not-exists with TTL).

column1: Why release a Redis lock via a Lua script?
column2: Owner check + delete must be atomic so you never delete someone else's re-acquired lock.

column1: How does Redlock acquire a lock?
column2: SETNX on N independent Redis masters; success if a majority (e.g. 3 of 5) is acquired, else release all.

column1: What does Redlock buy you and what does it cost?
column2: No single point of failure and better correctness; lower throughput (consensus is slow).

column1: Why do TTL-based locks need fencing tokens?
column2: A paused holder can outlive its TTL while another client acquires the lock; monotonically increasing tokens let the resource reject stale writers.

column1: Why can't sharded DBs rely on auto-increment IDs?
column2: Each independent shard's auto-increment collides with the others; the app must supply globally unique IDs.

column1: Why does epoch_ms alone fail as an ID?
column2: Two machines (or two calls) in the same millisecond produce the same value.

column1: How do you persist an ID counter cheaply and recover safely?
column2: Flush every N increments; on restart begin at last_flushed + N (+1), skipping but never reusing IDs.

column1: Why do ID schemes put time in the most significant bits?
column2: Numeric order matches time order (sortable); lower bits only break ties.

column1: What breaks monotonicity across machines?
column2: Clock skew between machines.

column1: Core lesson about distributed ID generation?
column2: You can't distribute it and guarantee strict monotonicity, so real systems relax a constraint.

column1: Amazon-style central ID service optimisation?
column2: Hand out ID batches (ranges) per call; servers re-ask when exhausted.

column1: Why avoid UUIDs as primary keys at scale?
column2: 128-bit random keys bloat indexes and scatter inserts; indexes stop fitting in memory.

column1: How do Flickr ticket servers work and avoid SPOF?
column2: MySQL auto-increment table bumped via upsert; two servers issue odd and even IDs.

column1: INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE vs REPLACE INTO?
column2: ODKU updates in place; REPLACE deletes then inserts (much slower). Both atomic.

column1: Snowflake bit layout?
column2: 41 bits epoch ms, 10 bits machine id, 12 bits per-machine sequence (plus a 0 sign bit).

column1: Instagram's ID layout and where it's generated?
column2: 41 bits ms since 2011, 13 bits logical shard, 10 bits sequence; a Postgres function at INSERT.

column1: Why is since_id pagination efficient?
column2: It seeks straight into the index (WHERE id > x LIMIT k) instead of skipping OFFSET rows.

column1: How does a CDN serve a request?
column2: Its domain maps to your origin; on a miss it fetches from the origin, caches the response and returns it.

column1: Why shouldn't photo uploads go through the API server?
column2: It doubles bandwidth and wastes API resources just relaying bytes.

column1: How does a client upload to S3 without your servers relaying?
column2: The service creates a pre-signed URL for an exact path; the client PUTs directly to S3.

column1: Why store image_id instead of the full image URL on a post?
column2: The S3 path is computable from user_id + image_id; saves space and lets the service validate ownership.

column1: How are Instagram's private photos protected?
column2: Short-lived signed CDN URLs; the CDN rejects invalid or expired signatures.

column1: Why can a service verify a JWT without the auth service?
column2: It checks the signature with the issuer's public key (asymmetric, e.g. RS256).

column1: When should you reach for public-key cryptography?
column2: When system A must trust system B's statement without calling B.

column1: How do you avoid sending huge photos to every device?
column2: CDN on-the-fly transformation (e.g. ?w=360), with cached variants.

column1: What is the Gravatar URL keyed by?
column2: A hash of the user's email.

column1: Two ways to model "one active photo per user"?
column2: is_active flag flipped in one transaction (with a unique partial index), or active_photo_id denormalised on users.

column1: How does the hashtag page achieve super-fast reads?
column2: One pre-computed document per tag (count + top posts), served by key from a partitioned DB, cache and CDN.

column1: Post ids vs full post details in the hashtag doc?
column2: Ids: small but N+1 enrichment on read. Full details: one fast read, more storage, risk of staleness.

column1: What's the value of splitting read and write paths?
column2: Each can be optimised independently: cache + thin API on reads; Kafka + batching on writes.

column1: How do hashtag workers count efficiently?
column2: Aggregate counts in memory and flush every N events or time window with one increment per tag.

column1: How do you minimise stop-the-world during a flush?
column2: Swap the active map under the lock (O(1)) and write the old map to the DB outside the lock.

column1: Why add a hashtag-extraction adapter?
column2: POST_PUBLISH is keyed by post; re-emitting per-hashtag events keyed by tag lets one consumer own each tag's counts.

column1: What does the newly-unread badge count?
column2: The number of distinct people with unread messages, not the number of messages.

column1: Best index for counting distinct unread senders?
column2: Covering composite (to, ts, from): equality, then range, then the read column.

column1: Day-N design for the unread indicator?
column2: ON_MSG_UNSENT events → workers SADD(dest, src) into a per-user Redis set; the badge is the set size; clear on read.

column1: How is "unread" detected in the pre-computed approach?
column2: The messaging service knows via WebSocket presence that delivery failed and emits ON_MSG_UNSENT.

column1: Core data structure of a cache server?
column2: A hash table mapping key → typed object (type decides allowed operations).

column1: HTTP vs raw TCP (RESP) for a cache?
column2: HTTP: easy tooling but heavy per-request overhead. RESP over TCP: minimal overhead, needs custom clients.

column1: How does a cache know it's full?
column2: Cap on key count, or track total bytes via an allocation wrapper (zmalloc/zfree).

column1: LRU vs LFU: typical workloads?
column2: LRU for recency-driven traffic (news, CDN); LFU for stable popularity (Wikipedia).

column1: Why does Redis approximate LRU?
column2: An exact doubly linked list costs memory and CPU; sampling keys into a small eviction pool is close enough.

column1: Three ways to expire TTL keys?
column2: Priority queue by expiry; lazy deletion on access; random sampling (Redis: 20 keys, repeat if > 25% expired).

column1: How does single-threaded Redis run background work?
column2: Time events in its event loop (serverCron, activeExpireCycle) interleaved with I/O.

column1: How do multi-threaded caches (DiceDB) avoid lock contention?
column2: Shared-nothing: one hash-table shard per core owned by a pinned data thread; I/O threads route by hash.

column1: Problem with hash(key) % N routing?
column2: Changing N remaps most keys (≈ N/(N+1) of them).

column1: How does consistent hashing assign keys?
column2: Nodes and keys hash onto a ring; each key goes to the next node clockwise.

column1: Steps to add a cache node with minimal transfer?
column2: Snapshot the neighbour, load, replicate until lag ≈ 0, brief pause, update ring, resume, delete moved data.

column1: What problem do virtual nodes solve?
column2: Skewed ring arcs: many positions per node spread load evenly.

column1: How do you look up a word in a 1 TB file quickly without a DB?
column2: Load a small word → (offset, length) index into memory and read only that byte range from S3.

column1: Rough size of the dictionary index?
column2: About 171k entries × ~16 B ≈ 2.7 MB (more with 8-byte offsets, still tiny).

column1: How is the weekly changelog applied efficiently?
column2: Both are sorted, so merge them in O(n) like merge sort, then rebuild the index.

column1: How do you switch dictionary versions without garbage reads?
column2: Upload to a new versioned path and flip a meta.json pointer; never overwrite files in place.

column1: How do you store index and data in one portable file?
column2: A fixed-length header holding the index and data offsets (plus metadata), followed by the index, then the data.

column1: Why are log-structured stores fast for writes?
column2: Append-only sequential writes avoid disk seeks.

column1: How does an append-only store delete a key?
column2: Append a tombstone (e.g. PUT(k, -1)); compaction removes it later.

column1: Layout of a Bitcask entry?
column2: CRC, timestamp, key size, value size, key, value.

column1: How does Bitcask achieve O(1) GET?
column2: An in-memory hash index maps key → (file id, value position, size); one seek reads the value.

column1: Bitcask's main limitation?
column2: All keys must fit in memory.

column1: What does merge/compaction do in Bitcask?
column2: Rewrites immutable files keeping only each key's latest live value and updates the index atomically.

column1: How do databases recover a torn write at the end of the log?
column2: Scan entries verifying CRCs and truncate at the first mismatch.

column1: Core idea of an LSM tree over Bitcask?
column2: Buffer writes in an in-memory memtable (plus a WAL), flush periodically to immutable sorted files, so keys needn't fit in RAM.

column1: What is an SSTable?
column2: An immutable file of key-sorted entries with an index of key → offset.

column1: Order of lookup for GET in an LSM?
column2: Memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest; first hit wins.

column1: Why flush the memtable to a new file each time?
column2: Faster, one-shot sequential writes; avoids rewriting a large existing file.

column1: How do Bloom filters speed up LSM reads?
column2: Each SSTable's filter says "definitely not here" so the file is skipped; "maybe" means check it.

column1: Bloom filter error types?
column2: False positives possible, false negatives impossible.

column1: Purpose of the WAL in an LSM?
column2: Durability for memtable contents; replayed on restart and truncated after each flush.

column1: B+ tree vs LSM workload fit?
column2: B+ trees for read-heavy; LSM for write-heavy.

column1: Name LSM-based storage engines.
column2: RocksDB, LevelDB, BadgerDB (also Cassandra).

column1: Idea behind multi-tiered order storage?
column2: Move orders to cheaper tiers by age (hot MySQL → S3) while keeping them queryable via indexes.

column1: How is cold data on S3 kept queryable?
column2: Indexed file layout (index + data) served by index servers or Athena/Hive-style engines.

column1: How do you ingest huge event volumes cheaply?
column2: Write to rotating local log files and ship them as batches to Kafka/S3, not one sync write per event.

column1: Why avoid video_id as the Kafka partition key for impressions?
column2: A viral video would create a hot partition; spread events evenly.

column1: Master vs playlist m3u8?
column2: Master lists renditions (bandwidth/resolution → playlist) and doesn't change; a playlist lists .ts segments and grows by appends during live.

column1: How does a player follow a live HLS stream?
column2: It periodically re-fetches the playlist and plays newly appended segments.

column1: SSAI vs CSAI?
column2: SSAI stitches ad segments into the manifest server-side (seamless, hard to block); CSAI plays ads in the client on cues (glitchy, blockable).

column1: Components of SSAI?
column2: Origin with SCTE-35 markers, a manifest manipulator, an ad decision server (VAST), and the CDN.

column1: How are private live streams protected at the CDN?
column2: Signed tokens/certificates validated by the CDN per request.

column1: Why use multiple CDNs?
column2: Backup and performance: continuously measure and shift traffic in real time.

column1: S3's four design goals?
column2: Strong consistency, global namespace, multi-tenancy, cost efficiency.

column1: What is a storage stamp?
column2: A cluster of 10–20 racks (~30–50 PB) run at ≤ 70% utilisation, with headroom for rack failures.

column1: What does the location service do?
column2: Maps accounts/namespaces to stamps (via DNS) and manages cross-stamp replication.

column1: Three layers inside a stamp?
column2: Front-end (auth + routing + streaming), Partition (range ownership, throttling), Stream (replicated append-only DFS).

column1: Why range partitioning in S3?
column2: Keeps object locality and tenant isolation, and lets hot ranges be split.

column1: Partition ownership rule?
column2: Each partition is owned by exactly one partition server; a server can own many partitions.

column1: How does S3-style storage get durability?
column2: Sync replicas within the stamp, async replicas across data centres and regions.

column1: Which user behaviours shape the recent-searches design?
column2: 50% tap the search bar within 5 s (read-heavy, must be preloaded); 30% of searches come from recent searches (write-heavy).

column1: How are recent searches stored for fast reads?
column2: A pre-computed list of the last 10 queries per user in Redis, written synchronously.

column1: Where does the full search history go?
column2: Async via Kafka into a partitioned NoSQL DB (search logs), archived to S3 after ~6 months.

column1: How do you avoid a slow first load when a user's Redis entry was evicted?
column2: Pre-warm recent searches into Redis when the app opens.

column1: Why short polling instead of WebSockets for Cricbuzz commentary?
column2: About one update per minute and identical data for everyone; cached polling is cheaper than millions of idle sockets.

column1: How is the latest commentary served cheaply?
column2: Redis holds the latest per match, or a CDN with max-age ≈ 5 s and prefreshing near expiry.

column1: How is commentary stored?
column2: Ball-wise rows (match_id, innings, ball, text), upserted per ball.

column1: Pain points of Day-0 Elasticsearch?
column2: Painful recovery, limits on scale and experimentation, hard debugging, no auto replication or latency routing, costly big tenants, no throttling.

column1: Key pieces of the revamped search platform?
column2: Indexers to primary + backup-region ES, a search gateway, identity (JWT) and relevance re-ranking, multi-region failover.

column1: ES routing strategy by tenant size?
column2: Small tenant → one shard (tenant_id % shards); large tenant → spread over N shards (tenant_id + doc_id % N).

column1: What problem does tenant-aware routing solve?
column2: Hot shards and noisy neighbours from uneven tenant sizes.

column1: Requirements of the distributed task scheduler?
column2: One-off or cron tasks executed (as HTTP calls) within a 30 s SLA, minute granularity, multi-tenant, ~2B tasks/day.

column1: Why must every scheduler component be horizontally scalable and fault tolerant?
column2: The strict SLA at extreme scale leaves no room for bottlenecks or single points of failure.

column1: How is the task store partitioned?
column2: By tenant (customer or microservice).

column1: What do task pullers do and how are they coordinated?
column2: Pull due tasks and enqueue them; each owns a tenant range assigned via ZooKeeper, reassigned if it dies.

column1: SQL used to pull due tasks concurrently?
column2: WHERE scheduled_at <= now AND picked_at IS NULL ORDER BY scheduled_at LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then mark picked.

column1: How are executors organised and scaled?
column2: Separate queues/fleets by priority and task type; an orchestrator autoscales on queue length.

column1: How are recurring (cron) tasks handled?
column2: Expand the cron into the next N absolute run times inserted as jobs (idempotently), topping up on each pick.

column1: Why model flash-sale stock as one row per unit?
column2: So concurrent buyers lock different rows (SKIP LOCKED) instead of all contending on one qty row.

column1: What happens on payment failure in the flash sale?
column2: The unit is released: picked_at and picked_by are reset to NULL.

column1: How are abandoned carts handled?
column2: A CRON job releases units picked more than ~12 min ago and not purchased.

column1: Why can't add-to-cart and payment be one transaction?
column2: They span services and time; there's no distributed transaction, so use steps with compensation.

column1: Why can't per-minute unique counts be summed?
column2: Users repeat across minutes; you need a set union, not a sum.

column1: Why are exact hash sets impractical for impression counting at scale?
column2: Each ad-minute can take MBs; hourly unions across thousands of customers run into TBs of processing.

column1: What data structure estimates unique counts cheaply?
column2: HyperLogLog (~12 KB per key, mergeable, approximate).

column1: Redis HLL commands?
column2: PFADD (add, O(1)), PFCOUNT (cardinality), PFMERGE (union of N HLLs).

column1: Main limitation of HLL besides approximation?
column2: You can't delete elements.

column1: How do you answer unique viewers for an arbitrary range?
column2: PFMERGE the per-minute HLLs for that range into a temp key, then PFCOUNT.

column1: How does the impressions design keep Redis small?
column2: Recent HLLs stay in Redis; bytes are copied periodically to DynamoDB and reloaded on demand.

column1: Why archive raw view events to S3?
column2: Replayability: if filter rules had a bug, events can be reprocessed.

column1: How does Dropbox represent a file?
column2: As a blocklist: hashes of 4 MB blocks, with blocks stored content-addressed.

column1: Dropbox upload protocol?
column2: Commit blocklist → metaserver replies with missing hashes → client uploads them to the block server → re-commit.

column1: How do clients learn about changes?
column2: A per-namespace incrementing version id; clients fetch everything after their last version, like a Kafka offset.

column1: How does multi-versioning fall out of the design?
column2: Old metadata rows keep old blocklists; the blocks still exist, so any version can be rebuilt.

column1: Why is geo-proximity hard with plain (x, y)?
column2: It needs a 2D range query (intersecting two 1D ranges), O(n) naively; 1D ranges are easy.

column1: How does GeoHash encode a location?
column2: Repeatedly halve the longitude and latitude ranges into bits, interleave them, and encode in base 32.

column1: What does a shared GeoHash prefix mean?
column2: The points fall in the same cell, so they're likely near each other (longer prefix = smaller cell).

column1: GeoHash boundary edge case and fix?
column2: Nearby points across a cell edge get different prefixes; also search the 8 neighbouring cells.

column1: Why Redis for ride-hailing driver locations?
column2: In-memory speed, built-in geo queries, multi-master multi-replica sharding.

column1: Why did Gojek need EVAL_RO?
column2: Redis rejects EVAL on replicas (scripts could write); a read-only variant lets filtering scripts run on replicas.

column1: How does the matcher keep latency low?
column2: Split the area into smaller GEOSEARCH queries run in parallel; return partial results if the SLA is breached.

column1: How were hot shards avoided for driver locations?
column2: Manually mix peak and low-traffic regions on each master (Redis sharding has no business context).

column1: Why not a graph DB for follow/following?
column2: No advanced graph algorithms needed; costly, hard to operate, and pagination is tricky.

column1: Problem with sharding an edges(src, dest) table by src?
column2: "Followers of B" filters on dest, so it must fan out across all shards.

column1: How do you serve both follower and following queries from one shard?
column2: Store two rows per follow, (A, B, FOLLOWS) and (B, A, FOLLOWED_BY), and shard by src.

column1: FlockDB primary key and unique index?
column2: PK (source_id, state, position); unique (source_id, destination_id, state).

column1: How does FlockDB paginate efficiently?
column2: Cursor on position (WHERE position > last ORDER BY position LIMIT k), not OFFSET.
